questions.title: Does Lisa’s “Okay” after the officer said he “need[ed] to come inside” count as voluntary consent or mere acquiescence to a claim of authority?
questions.question_body: The officer phrased his second request as, “I’m sensing that we almost need to come inside to make sure [the kids are okay],” and Lisa replied “Okay.” Under Bumper v. North Carolina, consent is invalid if it’s mere submission to a claim of lawful authority. How do courts distinguish a coercive “need to enter” statement (suggesting authority/exigency) from a permissible request for consent, especially in domestic-violence welfare checks? What facts here make Lisa’s “Okay” voluntary rather than acquiescence?

questions.title: How does the presence of body-camera footage affect the standard of review for the district court’s consent and scope findings?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Scott v. Harris and Norville to say video can “evaporate” factual disputes, but still says consent and scope are reviewed for clear error. When there’s body-cam video, does the Seventh Circuit ever treat some aspects of the interaction as effectively undisputed and thus review them de novo? Or is the presence of video just a reason why the appellate court is less likely to find clear error, without changing the formal standard?

questions.title: Could Georgia v. Randolph have limited the wife’s third-party consent because the husband was inside the home?
questions.question_body: The wife consented while the husband (defendant) was elsewhere in the house and hadn’t come to the door. Randolph bars warrantless entry with co-occupant consent if a physically present co-occupant objects. Does a co-occupant who is in another room count as “physically present” for Randolph purposes? Is an objection required to be contemporaneous and explicit at the threshold, and if the police don’t know the co-occupant’s position (or he’s not at the door), is the consenting spouse’s permission sufficient under Matlock?

questions.title: What defines the scope of consent in a domestic-violence welfare check when officers proceed to locate everyone and interview children?
questions.question_body: The court holds that entering to check the children’s welfare reasonably included scanning the home, locating the husband, and asking basic questions. Where’s the line between a permissible welfare check under consent and a search exceeding that consent? Would opening closed containers or looking in non-adjacent rooms be outside the scope? How do courts apply Florida v. Jimeno’s objective reasonableness test to welfare checks specifically, as opposed to vehicle or narcotics searches?

questions.title: If the initial entry were invalid, would the warrant based on the children’s statements be saved by independent source or attenuation?
questions.question_body: The officers obtained a warrant after speaking with the children inside during the consent-based entry. If that entry was unconstitutional, are the children’s statements (and the resulting warrant) automatically fruit of the poisonous tree, or could the government argue independent source, inevitable discovery, or attenuation? What would each doctrine require on these facts, and how have courts treated information from occupants obtained during welfare checks later used to support a warrant?

questions.title: Why didn’t the court reach exigent circumstances or inevitable discovery, and could the government have urged affirmance on those alternative grounds anyway?
questions.question_body: The panel says its consent holding makes it unnecessary to consider exigency and inevitable discovery. On appeal, can the government defend a suppression ruling on any ground supported by the record, even if the district court didn’t rely on it? If so, is the Seventh Circuit just exercising restraint here, or was the record underdeveloped for exigency/inevitable discovery analysis in domestic-violence 911 contexts?

questions.title: How do Schneckloth voluntariness factors apply when an occupant first refuses entry, then later consents after a short break?
questions.question_body: Lisa initially said she’d “prefer” officers not enter, went back inside, then later said “Okay.” The opinion emphasizes calm tone, short duration, and lack of custody. How do courts weigh: (1) an initial refusal followed by consent after repeated requests; (2) whether the person was advised of the right to refuse; and (3) the caretaker context of checking on children? Does an initial refusal generally strengthen the case for later voluntariness, or can it suggest pressure when officers persist?
